title: Salajeet, Shilajeet or Shilajit? Same Resin, Different Spellings
description: Salajeet, shilajeet, salajit and shilajit are the same substance spelled differently. Here is where each spelling comes from, and how to buy the real thing.
bodyHtml:
If you grew up in a Pakistani, Indian or Afghan household, you almost certainly heard it called salajeet. If you found it through a fitness forum, you probably know it as shilajit. Search either and you get different results, different sellers, and often wildly different prices, which leads a lot of people to assume they are looking at two different products.

They are not. Salajeet, shilajeet, salajit, shilajeet and shilajit are all the same mineral resin. The difference is transliteration, not substance.

Why there are so many spellings

The word has no single correct Latin spelling because it did not originate in a Latin alphabet. It comes into English from Sanskrit śilājatu, usually glossed as something close to "rock-born", and travelled outward through Persian, Urdu and Hindi, picking up local pronunciation along the way.

  • Shilajit: the most common English spelling, closest to the Sanskrit and Hindi pronunciation. This is what most Western retailers use.
  • Salajeet: the standard Urdu-derived spelling, and the one most widely used in Pakistan and across the British Pakistani community.
  • Shilajeet: a middle form, common in Indian English and in Ayurvedic writing.
  • Salajit and silajit: less common variants you will still see on packaging and in older texts.

None is more authentic than the others. A seller using "salajeet" is not selling you a different or better grade than one using "shilajit". They are usually just writing for a different audience.

Does the spelling tell you anything about the source?

Only loosely, and it is worth being careful here. Sellers using the Urdu spelling are more often sourcing from Pakistan, commonly Gilgit-Baltistan in the Karakoram range, while those using the Sanskrit-derived spelling more often source from the Indian Himalayas or Nepal. But this is a tendency, not a rule, and plenty of retailers pick the spelling with the better search volume rather than the one that matches their supply chain.

The honest position is that origin claims are only worth what the paperwork behind them is worth. "Gilgit shilajit" and "pure salajeet from the Karakoram" are marketing phrases unless the seller can point to something verifiable. Geography does not substitute for testing.

What actually determines quality

Regardless of what it is called on the jar, the same three things separate good resin from bad:

Purification

Raw shilajit is not edible. It comes out of the rock mixed with soil, plant debris and mineral contamination, and it has to be purified before it is safe. Traditional methods use water filtration and sun-drying; industrial ones use heat and solvents, which can be harsher on the compounds inside. Raw, unprocessed resin should never be taken directly.

Heavy metals testing

This is the one that matters most and gets discussed least. Because shilajit forms in rock, it can carry lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury from its source material. Purification is what removes them, and a third-party heavy metals report is the only way to confirm it worked. Ask for one that names the batch, not a generic certificate from a previous year.

How it behaves

Properly purified resin softens in the hand, dissolves cleanly in warm water within about a minute, and turns the liquid a dark amber-brown. Grit at the bottom of the glass, bits that refuse to dissolve, or a product that stays rock-hard at room temperature are all reasons to stop and ask questions.

Buying salajeet in the UK and Europe

A lot of salajeet reaches British and European households informally, brought back in a suitcase, or bought from a shop that gets it from someone who gets it from someone. That chain is often perfectly fine and often genuinely cheaper. It is also completely untested, which means you are trusting a chain of people you cannot see.

If you would rather not do that, the things to look for are the same ones you would apply to any supplement: a real registered business, a published batch report, a shipping origin that does not land you with an unexpected customs bill, and a seller who will answer a direct question about sourcing without deflecting.

Our own certificates are published in full on our About page, downloadable, no email required. If you are buying within the EU, our guide to buying shilajit in Europe covers customs and shipping in more detail.

A note on how it is sold

Salajeet has a long history in South Asian traditional medicine, and you will find it described in some very confident terms, particularly in marketing aimed at men. It is worth separating that from what is actually established. In the UK and EU, shilajit is regulated as a food supplement, which means it cannot legally be sold as a treatment for any condition, and claims about what it does to the body have to come from an authorised list. Where a seller is making dramatic promises, that is a reason for more scepticism, not less.

The short version

Salajeet, shilajeet and shilajit are the same thing. Search whichever spelling comes naturally to you. Then ignore the word on the label entirely and ask the only question that separates one jar from another: can you show me the lab report for this batch?

If you want the background on how the resin forms and where it comes from, our guide to what shilajit actually is covers it properly. For dosage and method, see how to take shilajit.

This article is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Shilajit is a food supplement and is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease. Please consult a qualified healthcare professional before starting any new supplement, particularly if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, taking medication or managing a health condition.
